architectural_implications.after: A 7-step pipeline (Questions, Research, Design, Structure Outline, Plan, Worktree, Implement, PR) with per-step prompts under 40 instructions and sequencing expressed as control flow.
architectural_implications.before: One monolithic prompt carrying research, planning, and sequencing instructions plus full ticket context.
architectural_implications.consequence: Each step has a small, auditable instruction surface; failures localize to a step, and the human gets checkpoints to review before the next stage runs.
architectural_implications.observation: Orchestration was embedded in a single create_plan mega-prompt with 85+ instructions.

architectural_implications.after: Research runs on de-ticketed, neutral context; the ticket informs later design/plan steps.
architectural_implications.before: Research prompt receives the ticket plus system context in one blob.
architectural_implications.consequence: Reduces confirmation bias in research output and yields findings that reflect system reality rather than the requester's framing.
architectural_implications.observation: Context from the intent artifact (the ticket) was mixed into the investigation step.

architectural_implications.after: Plans constrained to vertical phases with explicit checkpoints and continuous testing.
architectural_implications.before: Model-authored horizontal plans executing all DB, then all API, then all frontend.
architectural_implications.consequence: Errors surface at slice boundaries instead of after large horizontal batches, cutting rework and making agent output reviewable.
architectural_implications.observation: Planning granularity was a free choice left to the model.

article_ideas.angle: Reframe context engineering as a zero-sum accounting problem and show why non-local agent failures appear as frameworks grow.
article_ideas.audience: AI platform and developer-tooling engineers running shared agent harnesses
article_ideas.thesis: System prompts, project memory files, tool schemas, and MCP integrations all spend from the same finite instruction-following capacity, so adding any of them silently degrades compliance with workflow instructions that were never edited. Context engineering is therefore budget allocation, and platform teams need a ledger before they need more capabilities.
article_ideas.title: Your Agent Has One Instruction Budget, Not Many

article_ideas.angle: Show that the primary lever for agent reliability is architectural relocation of control flow rather than better prompt craft.
article_ideas.audience: Engineers designing multi-step agent pipelines and internal coding-agent platforms
article_ideas.based_on: use deterministic control flow (if statements, loops) to manage agent pipelines
article_ideas.thesis: Sequencing, branching, and retries belong in deterministic harness code, not in natural-language instructions. Control logic written in prose both consumes the instruction budget the task itself needs and is non-deterministic, which is why splitting a mega-prompt into discrete steps improved adherence more than any prompt rewrite did.
article_ideas.title: Move the Loop Out of the Prompt

article_ideas.angle: Treat phase ordering as a review gate, not a planning preference, and tie it directly to bug-localization cost.
article_ideas.audience: Tech leads and reviewers adopting coding agents on existing codebases
article_ideas.based_on: Models love writing horizontal plans which are hard to debug
article_ideas.thesis: Models default to horizontal plans, which hide wrong assumptions until large amounts of code already exist. Enforcing small end-to-end phases with checkpoints is what makes agent output reviewable and bounds rework, so plan granularity should be a validated structural property of the plan artifact rather than a stylistic preference.
article_ideas.title: Vertical Slices Are the Unit of Agent Review

article_ideas.angle: Attack the default measurement of agent productivity and propose deployment gating by task type.
article_ideas.audience: Engineering leaders and productivity researchers evaluating AI coding rollouts
article_ideas.based_on: AI use in software engineering increases rework
article_ideas.thesis: AI assistance raises code output while also raising rework, and its value is conditional on task complexity rather than uniform. Any productivity claim built on throughput alone will look like a win while the cleanup cost lands in a later period, so teams need rework-inclusive, complexity-segmented metrics and a rule for which task types agents should touch at all.
article_ideas.title: Output Volume Is a Vanity Metric for Coding Agents

connections.relationship: Every context artifact (system prompt, project memory file, tool/MCP schema) draws from one shared, finite instruction-following capacity, so context engineering becomes budget allocation.
Moving sequencing and branching into deterministic code is the primary mechanism for freeing instruction budget for the task itself.
Both create reviewable checkpoints (interface contract, phase boundary) that force alignment before expensive generation, bounding rework.
Checkpoints are the point at which broken assumptions are detected, restoring the human inspection loop that agent delegation tends to bypass.
Rework cost is conditional on greenfield vs brownfield complexity, so agent deployment should be gated by task type rather than applied uniformly.

evidence_quotes.text: Referencing research showing frontier LLMs can only follow 150 to 200 instructions with reasonable consistency.
Combining system prompts, claudemd, tools, and MCPs exhausts the instruction budget

core_insights.generalization: Any agent runtime that stacks system prompt + project context + tool schemas + retrieved instructions should budget total instruction count globally and treat each addition as spending from the same account.
core_insights.insight: The instruction budget is a single finite resource shared across system prompts, CLAUDE.md-style context files, tool definitions, and MCP integrations — not a per-prompt limit. Frontier LLMs follow roughly 150-200 instructions consistently, so every added tool schema or context file consumes budget that the task workflow needs.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It reframes context/tool/instruction design as a zero-sum allocation problem: adding an MCP or a memory file silently degrades compliance with existing workflow instructions, which explains non-local agent failures as frameworks grow.

evidence_quotes.text: Instead of putting all control logic inside long prompts, use deterministic control flow (if statements, loops) to manage agent pipelines
Splitting a single mega-prompt into discrete agent steps reduced instructions from 85+ to under 40

core_insights.generalization: Pipeline structure belongs in the harness; prompts should specify only the narrow task for the current step. This applies to any multi-step agent workflow, not just coding.
core_insights.insight: Agent orchestration logic should live in deterministic control flow (if statements, loops, discrete steps) rather than inside long prompts. Splitting one mega-prompt into discrete agent steps cut per-prompt instructions from 85+ to under 40.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Moves sequencing, branching, and retry responsibility out of natural-language instructions and into code, where it is inspectable, testable, and not subject to instruction-budget decay.

evidence_quotes.text: Models love writing horizontal plans which are hard to debug
Vertical plans provide checkpoints and enable early detection of broken assumptions
Writing 1200 lines of horizontal code across database, services, and frontend in one go.

core_insights.generalization: Incremental, verifiable slice ordering is a general principle for any agent-generated execution plan, including infra and data-pipeline agents.
core_insights.insight: Plans must be decomposed into vertical slices (small end-to-end phases with checkpoints and continuous testing) rather than horizontal layers (all DB, then all API, then all frontend). Models default to writing horizontal plans, which are hard to debug.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Vertical phasing surfaces broken assumptions at each checkpoint, bounding the blast radius of a wrong decision and making agent output reviewable; horizontal plans hide errors until thousands of lines are already written.

evidence_quotes.text: People were getting bad research because tickets were mixed with research context
Hide the raw ticket from research context to maintain objectivity

core_insights.generalization: Separate the artifact that defines intent from the agent step that investigates reality; feed the investigation a neutral framing to avoid confirmation bias in any research/extraction agent.
core_insights.insight: Contaminating the research step with the raw ticket context produces biased, low-quality research; hiding the ticket from the research context preserves objectivity.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It identifies an input-hygiene failure mode: giving the agent the intended answer inside the investigation step causes it to rationalize toward the ticket rather than discover the actual system state.

evidence_quotes.text: Using structure outlines as C header files equivalent for AI plans
Encourages human-agent mental alignment before writing code

core_insights.generalization: Agent pipelines for large changes benefit from an explicit interface/signature artifact as an intermediate gate between design and implementation, verifiable independently of the code.
core_insights.insight: A 'structure outline' precursor artifact (an interface/header-file equivalent) is produced before the full implementation plan, acting as a reviewable contract between design and implementation.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Inserts a cheap, human-reviewable interface layer where the human-agent mental alignment check happens, catching structural disagreement before expensive plan and code generation.

evidence_quotes.text: AI increases code output volume
AI use in software engineering increases rework
Great for low-complexity greenfield tasks, poor for high-complexity brownfield tasks

core_insights.generalization: Agent productivity should be measured with rework-inclusive metrics and segmented by task complexity, not by output volume.
core_insights.insight: AI assistance increases code output volume (~50%) while also increasing rework, and its value is complexity-dependent: strong on low-complexity greenfield work, weak on high-complexity brownfield work.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Gives a task-complexity selection criterion for where to deploy coding agents and cautions that throughput metrics alone mask downstream cleanup cost.

Maintain code ownership and review intermediate markdown artifacts

core_insights.generalization: Any agentic pipeline that removes human inspection of intermediate and final artifacts accumulates latent structural debt that surfaces only at rewrite scale.
core_insights.insight: Six months of delegating without reading code produced systemic failures requiring major rewrites; plans do not substitute for code and artifact review.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Establishes that reviewing intermediate markdown artifacts and reading generated code are load-bearing, not optional ceremony, and that code ownership must survive agent adoption.

deep_dives.why: If all context artifacts draw from one finite instruction-following account, then a platform team adding an MCP or a memory file is silently spending the budget the workflow needs. Without per-source accounting and adherence telemetry, that degradation is invisible until agents start skipping steps, and no allocation policy can be defended.

evidence_quotes.text: Using structure outlines as C header files equivalent for AI plans

deep_dives.why: Plan quality is named as a central failure source, yet the only remedies offered are structural heuristics. A structure outline is an independently checkable artifact sitting between design and implementation, so it is the natural anchor for a verification pass that converts plan review from taste into a falsifiable gate.

evidence_quotes.text: Models love writing horizontal plans which are hard to debug

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Models love writing horizontal plans which are hard to debug
deep_dives.why: It determines whether planning granularity is a prompt-wording problem or a harness-constraint problem. evidence_quotes.text: Combining system prompts, claudemd, tools, and MCPs exhausts the instruction budget

deep_dives.trigger_insight: Hide the raw ticket from research context to maintain objectivity
deep_dives.why: The practice is asserted as a rule but reported without outcome measurement. If it does not change downstream defects, an entire step-independent input discipline is being enforced on aesthetic grounds, which is costly and hard to sustain across thousands of engineers.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Dexter Horthy
  • Channel: AAIF Live
  • Main topic: Lessons learned from rolling out Research-Plan-Implement (RPI) and QR-SPI methodology for AI coding agents to thousands of engineers.
  • Purpose: To share hard-earned production lessons on how to effectively use AI coding agents without sacrificing code quality or overwhelming instruction budgets. Dexter Horthy discusses the mistakes made over six months of building and deploying AI coding agents using the Research-Plan-Implement (RPI) and QR-SPI methodologies. He examines Stanford developer productivity studies, instruction budgets for LLMs, why monolithic prompts fail, the danger of bad research and bad plans, the difference between horizontal and vertical planning, and the importance of human-agent mental alignment.

Topic Map

Stanford Developer Productivity Study

  • Explanation: Reviewing Igor's Stanford study on AI developer productivity, showing that while AI increases output volume by ~50%, it also significantly increases rework and fixing mess from last week, especially on high-complexity brownfield tasks.
  • Key claims:
    • AI increases code output volume
    • AI use in software engineering increases rework
    • Great for low-complexity greenfield tasks, poor for high-complexity brownfield tasks
  • Examples:
    • Greenfield vs brownfield task execution
  • Terminology:
    • rework
    • greenfield
    • brownfield
    • task complexity
  • Why it matters: Understanding the limits of AI productivity prevents teams from shipping buggy code under the illusion of speed.

What Went Wrong with RPI

  • Explanation: Examining why initial RPI (Research, Plan, Implement) prompts and commands failed for many teams when deployed broadly.
  • Key claims:
    • People were getting bad research because tickets were mixed with research context
    • Plans were low quality due to giant monolithic prompts with 85+ instructions
    • Models cannot follow hundreds of instructions reliably
  • Examples:
    • Passing full ticket context directly into research step
  • Terminology:
    • instruction budget
    • monolithic prompt
    • compression of truth
  • Why it matters: Highlights why prompt engineering alone is insufficient without proper structural workflow design.

The Instruction Budget

  • Explanation: Referencing research showing frontier LLMs can only follow 150 to 200 instructions with reasonable consistency.
  • Key claims:
    • Exceeding 150-200 instructions drops adherence significantly
    • Combining system prompts, claudemd, tools, and MCPs exhausts the instruction budget
  • Examples:
    • 85+ instructions in a single create_plan prompt
  • Terminology:
    • instruction budget
    • frontier LLMs
    • consistency
  • Why it matters: Explains why agent frameworks break down as instructions grow.

Horizontal vs Vertical Plans

  • Explanation: Contrasting horizontal plans (doing all DB, then all API, then all frontend) with vertical plans (phases touching small vertical slices with continuous testing).
  • Key claims:
    • Models love writing horizontal plans which are hard to debug
    • Vertical plans provide checkpoints and enable early detection of broken assumptions
  • Examples:
    • 1200 lines of code written horizontally vs partitioned into vertical phases
  • Terminology:
    • horizontal plans
    • vertical plans
    • checkpoints
  • Why it matters: Vertical planning drastically reduces rework and makes agent output reviewable.

The 7-Step QR-SPI Process

  • Explanation: Introducing the evolved Q-R-S-P-I (Questions, Research, Design, Structure Outline, Plan, Worktree, Implement, Pull Request) acronym known as Crispy.
  • Key claims:
    • Splitting monolithic prompts into 7 distinct steps keeps instructions per prompt under 40
    • Encourages human-agent mental alignment before writing code
  • Examples:
    • Using structure outlines as C header files equivalent for AI plans
  • Terminology:
    • QR-SPI
    • Crispy
    • structure outline
    • design concept
  • Why it matters: Provides a robust, scalable engineering framework for AI-driven development.

Key Points

Do not outsource the thinking

  • Explanation: Engineers must remain actively involved in design and alignment rather than relying on a magic prompt.
  • Evidence: User feedback across thousands of engineers showing poor results when agents make all decisions autonomously.
  • Practical implication: Engineers should use agents for leverage while retaining ownership of architectural intent.

Read the code

  • Explanation: Despite initial thoughts that plans eliminate code reading, teams must still read code and plans.
  • Evidence: Six months of not reading code led to systemic failures requiring major rewrites.
  • Practical implication: Maintain code ownership and review intermediate markdown artifacts.

Control flow over prompt instructions

  • Explanation: Instead of putting all control logic inside long prompts, use deterministic control flow (if statements, loops) to manage agent pipelines.
  • Evidence: Splitting a single mega-prompt into discrete agent steps reduced instructions from 85+ to under 40.
  • Practical implication: Build agent pipelines with structured code rather than complex prompt steering.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

QR-SPI (Crispy)

  • How it works: A multi-step agentic workflow breaking down software engineering tasks into discrete, verifiable phases.
  • Components:
    • Questions
    • Research
    • Design
    • Structure Outline
    • Plan
    • Worktree
    • Implement
    • Pull Request
  • When to use: When building complex software systems with AI coding agents to ensure high quality and alignment.

Examples & Case Studies

Teams giving monolithic prompts with 85+ instructions to coding agents.

  • Illustrates: Instruction budget exhaustion leading to skipped steps and low-quality plans.
  • Lesson: Split prompts into smaller, focused sub-tasks and use control flow.

Writing 1200 lines of horizontal code across database, services, and frontend in one go.

  • Illustrates: Difficulty in localizing bugs when nothing is tested incrementally.
  • Lesson: Use vertical plans with intermediate checkpoints.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Keep instructions per prompt under 40
    • Use structure outlines before writing full implementation plans
    • Hide the raw ticket from research context to maintain objectivity
  • Strategic:
    • Avoid monolithic mega-prompts
    • Embrace human-agent mental alignment through design discussions
    • Design agent pipelines using programmatic control flow
  • Questions to investigate:
    • How do we formally verify agent-generated plans?
    • What is the optimal instruction budget for domain-specific coding agents?
    • How do we measure developer productivity improvements accurately with AI?

Claims Worth Verifying

  • Frontier LLMs can only follow 150-200 instructions with reasonable consistency. (empirical)
  • Using AI in software engineering increases rework by 50%. (empirical)

Notable Quotes

"I am humble enough to admit when I was wrong." "Do not outsource the thinking." "If you built a tool that requires 7+ hours of training to wield, go fix the tool."

Compressed Summary

  • RPI methodology evolved into QR-SPI (Crispy) to handle instruction budgets.
  • Monolithic prompts exceeding 150 instructions fail consistently.
  • Vertical planning and intermediate markdown docs prevent agent drift and rework.
  • Human-agent mental alignment requires collaborative design before implementation.
  • Keywords: coding agents, rpi, qr-spi, context engineering, instruction budget
  • Core insight: To make AI coding agents reliable, engineers must manage instruction budgets by splitting monolithic prompts into structured, vertical workflows with continuous human-agent alignment.

  - Splitting monolithic prompts into 7 distinct steps keeps instructions per prompt under 40
  - Encourages human-agent mental alignment before writing code
- **Examples**:
  - Using structure outlines as C header files equivalent for AI plans
- **Terminology**:
  - QR-SPI
  - Crispy
  - structure outline
  - design concept
- **Why it matters**: Provides a robust, scalable engineering framework for AI-driven development.
## Key Points
### Do not outsource the thinking
- **Explanation**: Engineers must remain actively involved in design and alignment rather than relying on a magic prompt.
- **Evidence**: User feedback across thousands of engineers showing poor results when agents make all decisions autonomously.
- **Practical implication**: Engineers should use agents for leverage while retaining ownership of architectural intent.
### Read the code
- **Explanation**: Despite initial thoughts that plans eliminate code reading, teams must still read code and plans.
- **Evidence**: Six months of not reading code led to systemic failures requiring major rewrites.
- **Practical implication**: Maintain code ownership and review intermediate markdown artifacts.
### Control flow over prompt instructions
- **Explanation**: Instead of putting all control logic inside long prompts, use deterministic control flow (if statements, loops) to manage agent pipelines.
- **Evidence**: Splitting a single mega-prompt into discrete agent steps reduced instructions from 85+ to under 40.
- **Practical implication**: Build agent pipelines with structured code rather than complex prompt steering.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### QR-SPI (Crispy)
- **How it works**: A multi-step agentic workflow breaking down software engineering tasks into discrete, verifiable phases.
- **Components**:
  - Questions
  - Research
  - Design
  - Structure Outline
  - Plan
  - Worktree
  - Implement
  - Pull Request
- **When to use**: When building complex software systems with AI coding agents to ensure high quality and alignment.
## Examples & Case Studies
### Teams giving monolithic prompts with 85+ instructions to coding agents.
- **Illustrates**: Instruction budget exhaustion leading to skipped steps and low-quality plans.
- **Lesson**: Split prompts into smaller, focused sub-tasks and use control flow.
### Writing 1200 lines of horizontal code across database, services, and frontend in one go.
- **Illustrates**: Difficulty in localizing bugs when nothing is tested incrementally.
- **Lesson**: Use vertical plans with intermediate checkpoints.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Keep instructions per prompt under 40
  - Use structure outlines before writing full implementation plans
  - Hide the raw ticket from research context to maintain objectivity
- **Strategic**:
  - Avoid monolithic mega-prompts
  - Embrace human-agent mental alignment through design discussions
  - Design agent pipelines using programmatic control flow
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - How do we formally verify agent-generated plans?
  - What is the optimal instruction budget for domain-specific coding agents?
  - How do we measure developer productivity improvements accurately with AI?
## Claims Worth Verifying
- Frontier LLMs can only follow 150-200 instructions with reasonable consistency. (empirical)
- Using AI in software engineering increases rework by 50%. (empirical)
## Notable Quotes
> "I am humble enough to admit when I was wrong."
> "Do not outsource the thinking."
> "If you built a tool that requires 7+ hours of training to wield, go fix the tool."
## Compressed Summary
- RPI methodology evolved into QR-SPI (Crispy) to handle instruction budgets.
- Monolithic prompts exceeding 150 instructions fail consistently.
- Vertical planning and intermediate markdown docs prevent agent drift and rework.
- Human-agent mental alignment requires collaborative design before implementation.
- **Keywords**: coding agents, rpi, qr-spi, context engineering, instruction budget
- **Core insight**: To make AI coding agents reliable, engineers must manage instruction budgets by splitting monolithic prompts into structured, vertical workflows with continuous human-agent alignment.
